description_full: Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. owns, manufactures, and distributors beverages and single serve brewing systems in the United States and internationally. The company operates through three segments: U.S. Refreshment Beverages, U.S. Coffee, and International. It manufactures and distributes branded concentrates, syrup, and finished beverages, as well as sales of owned brands and third-party brands; tea, cocoa, and other products; and offers finished goods relating to K-Cup pods, single serve brewers, specialty coffee, and ready to drink coffee products. The company offers its products under the Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, Mott's, A&W, Peñafiel, GHOST, Snapple, 7UP, Green Mountain Coffee Roasters, Clamato, Core Hydration, The Original Donut Shop, Sunkist soda, Squirt, C4 Energy, Hawaiian Punch, Electrolit, Bloom, Bai, Evian, Yoo-Hoo, Vita Coco, Big Red, RC Cola, Crush, McCafé, Tim Hortons, Van Houtte, Celestial Seasonings, Bigelow, Starbucks, Dunkin', Folgers, Peet's, and Swiss Miss brands, as well as other partner and private label brands. It markets and sells its products to supermarkets, mass merchandisers, club stores, e-commerce retailers, office superstores, vending machines, fountains, grocery and drug stores, convenience stores, and other small outlets; and directly to consumers through Keurig.com website. Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. was founded in 1981 and is headquartered in Frisco, Texas.

financial_summary: Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $49.9B market cap on $16.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 58% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.5B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.96× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.8× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.0×.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.7% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.

In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 12% in the 2022 bear market and 55% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $32.74 (margin of safety -12%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $22.00 to $49.18 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 33.0 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 17.3 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 33.1 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 4% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $38.03 on average, 4% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% earns above the cost of capital of 6.0%, but the 0pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.52).
It runs a 58% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.8x net debt to EBITDA ($1.0B of cash against $16.1B of debt), with interest covered 6.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.59 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.64 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-24 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.7% over 3 years, 7.4% over 5 years and 10.2% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 40% of profits supports about 2.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 2.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.7%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 3 sales over the past year, net $839K sold.
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (0.0% in buybacks and 2.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 16 consecutive years, raising it 8.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 50,000 employees, each generates about $332K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 7.5% a year.
